item.text: {"text":"HR@10 with 99 sampled negatives measures whether the held-out item reaches the top 10 among 100 candidates; it does not establish full-catalog ranking quality or real-world intent. Krichene and Rendle show sampled metrics can reverse model ordering relative to full-catalog metrics, even in expectation ([study](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/)). With 200 users/category, one changed hit moves category HR by 0.5 percentage points and the four-category macro average by 0.125 points. Small gains can therefore depend on few users. Repeatedly choosing architectures, checkpoints and hyperparameters against the same validation set also creates selection optimism; adaptive holdout research shows reuse can overfit validation itself ([Dwork et al.](https://papers.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2015/hash/bad5f33780c42f2588878a9d07405083-Abstract.html)).\n\nKeep the pinned evaluator unchanged. Compare models on identical users and candidates using per-user hit differences: +1 for a gained hit, −1 for a lost hit, 0 otherwise. Report gains/losses, category differences and their equal-weight macro average. A paired bootstrap resampling users within each category can describe uncertainty in the macro difference; an exact McNemar test can assess category-level discordant outcomes. These analyses condition on the fixed candidate draws and fitted models: they do not capture candidate-sampling or training variation, establish intent, or remove adaptive-selection bias. Log every proposal, checkpoint evaluation, validation query, failure, GPU-second cost and selection rule, including unsuccessful trials. Label winner-versus-baseline intervals exploratory after selection; transparent accounting exposes search intensity without claiming to correct it or accessing test labels."}
